title: ZzzQuil and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Risks, Timing and Alternatives
excerpt: Can you take ZzzQuil after drinking? How diphenhydramine and alcohol stack up in your brain, whether ZzzQuil contains alcohol, how long to wait, and safer ways to sleep after a night out.
metaDescription: Can you take ZzzQuil after drinking? How diphenhydramine and alcohol interact, whether ZzzQuil has alcohol, how long to wait, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** you shouldn't take ZzzQuil on a night you've been drinking. ZzzQuil's main sleep ingredient is diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine, and the product's own label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks while using it. Both diphenhydramine and alcohol slow your brain down, and together they add up. The usual result is heavier sedation, worse coordination, a foggier memory and a rougher morning. At higher doses, or after a lot of alcohol, the combination can become genuinely dangerous. This guide explains why, answers the common question of whether ZzzQuil itself contains alcohol, and covers how long to wait and what to do instead if you can't sleep after a night out.

**The quick rules:** If you've had alcohol tonight, skip ZzzQuil and any other "PM" or nighttime sleep product. Wait until the alcohol is fully out of your system before using it. Never take more than the labeled dose to "push through" alcohol-disrupted sleep. Check every other medicine you've taken for diphenhydramine or doxylamine so you don't double up. And if someone has mixed sleep aids with heavy drinking and is hard to wake, breathing slowly, vomiting while drowsy or confused, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general pharmacology and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and medications. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before combining any sleep aid with alcohol, and see a doctor if** you regularly need a sleep aid to sleep after drinking, you're over 65, you're pregnant or breastfeeding, you take other sedating medicines (such as antidepressants, anxiety medicines, opioids, muscle relaxants or other antihistamines), or you have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, asthma or other breathing problems. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** if someone who has mixed alcohol with a sleep aid can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, is vomiting while very drowsy, or seems severely confused. In the US, Poison Control is available at **1-800-222-1222**.

## What Is Actually in ZzzQuil?

ZzzQuil is a Vicks brand, and the name covers two quite different kinds of product. It matters which one you have.

- **ZzzQuil Nighttime Sleep-Aid (the original liquid and LiquiCaps).** The active ingredient is **diphenhydramine HCl**, the same drug found in Benadryl. A standard adult dose is 50 mg (for example, two 25 mg LiquiCaps or one labeled dose of the liquid). This is the product the alcohol warning is mainly about.
- **ZzzQuil Pure Zzzs.** This is a separate line of supplements built around **melatonin**, usually combined with botanicals such as lavender, chamomile or valerian. It contains no diphenhydramine. It's sold as a dietary supplement rather than an over-the-counter drug.

Diphenhydramine has been around since the 1940s. It was developed as an allergy medicine, and drowsiness was its best-known side effect. Sleep-aid brands simply turned that side effect into the main purpose. That history is useful to remember, because ZzzQuil is not a special sleep molecule. It's an old, strong antihistamine with all the baggage that comes with one.

Always read the Drug Facts box on your specific package. Formulas, strengths and flavors change over time and vary between countries.

## Does ZzzQuil Have Alcohol in It?

This is one of the most searched questions about the product, mostly because people mix it up with NyQuil.

**The standard ZzzQuil Nighttime Sleep-Aid liquid is made without alcohol.** Its inactive ingredients are things like water, glycerin, propylene glycol, sweeteners, flavors and preservatives. The LiquiCaps don't contain drinking alcohol either. That said, inactive ingredient lists do change, so the reliable move is to check the label on your bottle rather than trust any website, including this one.

**NyQuil is a different story.** The original NyQuil liquid has long contained alcohol as an inactive ingredient (the label lists it at 10%), and Vicks sells a separate "alcohol-free" NyQuil for people who want to avoid it. The confusion between the two is understandable, since the names and packaging are similar.

Here's the important point, though. **Whether ZzzQuil contains alcohol is not the real safety issue.** The problem is the diphenhydramine. Even a completely alcohol-free sleep aid becomes risky when you add it on top of the alcohol you drank that evening. An alcohol-free label tells you about what's in the bottle. It tells you nothing about what's already in your bloodstream.

## Why ZzzQuil and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Mechanism in Plain Words

### Two brakes on the same system

Your brain runs on a balance between signals that keep you alert and signals that calm things down. Both alcohol and diphenhydramine push toward "calm down," but they do it in different ways.

- **Alcohol** boosts the effect of GABA, the brain's main calming chemical, and dampens glutamate, one of its main excitatory chemicals. That's why a drink or two feels relaxing, and why a lot of drinks causes slurred speech, poor balance and blackouts.
- **Diphenhydramine** blocks histamine H1 receptors in the brain. Histamine is one of the chemicals that keeps you awake, so blocking it makes you drowsy. Unlike newer allergy pills such as loratadine (Claritin), diphenhydramine crosses easily into the brain, which is exactly why it sedates.

When you combine them, you're pressing two different brakes on the same system at once. Pharmacologists call this **additive central nervous system (CNS) depression**, which just means the slowing effects stack. You don't get "a bit sleepier." You can get much more impaired than you'd expect from either one alone.

### The anticholinergic problem

Diphenhydramine also blocks acetylcholine, a chemical involved in memory, attention, and many automatic body functions. This is called an **anticholinergic** effect. It's responsible for many of diphenhydramine's side effects:

- Dry mouth and dry eyes
- Blurred vision
- Constipation and trouble urinating
- Confusion, poor memory and slowed thinking
- A fast heartbeat

Alcohol affects memory and judgment too, so the two together can make confusion and memory gaps worse. In older adults, anticholinergic drugs are already linked to confusion and falls. That's why diphenhydramine is on the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria list of medicines that older adults should generally avoid. Adding alcohol makes that risk worse.

### What the combination can do

At a normal dose of ZzzQuil after one drink, a healthy adult will probably just feel very sedated and groggy the next morning. The risks grow as the amount of alcohol and medicine goes up:

- **Heavy sedation and poor coordination.** This raises the chance of falls, especially getting up to use the bathroom in the night.
- **Impaired judgment and memory.** You may not remember taking a dose, which can lead to taking another.
- **Vomiting while deeply sedated.** Heavy drinking often causes nausea. If you're too sedated to wake up properly, there's a real risk of choking on vomit. This is one of the most serious dangers of mixing any sedative with a lot of alcohol.
- **Slowed breathing.** At high doses, combined CNS depressants can suppress breathing. This is more of a concern with large amounts of alcohol or with other sedatives in the mix.
- **Next-day impairment.** Driving or operating machinery the next morning can be unsafe, even if you feel mostly fine.

In overdose, diphenhydramine on its own can cause severe confusion, hallucinations, seizures and dangerous heart rhythm problems. Alcohol doesn't cause these specific effects, but by clouding your judgment it makes accidental overdose more likely.

## What the ZzzQuil Label Says About Alcohol

You don't need to rely on anyone's opinion here. The Drug Facts label on diphenhydramine sleep aids sold in the US spells out the key warnings. They typically include:

- **"When using this product avoid alcoholic drinks."**
- Ask a doctor or pharmacist before use if you are taking sedatives or tranquilizers.
- Do not use with any other product containing diphenhydramine, even one used on the skin.
- Ask a doctor before use if you have glaucoma, trouble urinating due to an enlarged prostate, or breathing problems such as emphysema or chronic bronchitis.
- Not for use in children under 12.
- If sleeplessness persists for more than two weeks, see a doctor, since it may be a sign of a serious underlying illness.

That last point matters for people who reach for a sleep aid every time they drink. Needing a pill to sleep after drinking, again and again, is worth a conversation with a doctor.

## Why ZzzQuil Doesn't Fix Alcohol-Ruined Sleep

Most people who think about taking ZzzQuil after drinking have a good reason: they've noticed that alcohol wrecks their sleep. They fall asleep fast, then wake at 3 or 4 a.m. feeling wired, sweaty or restless and can't get back to sleep. It makes sense to want something to get through the second half of the night.

The problem is that the sleep aid doesn't treat what's actually going on.

### What alcohol does to your sleep

Alcohol helps you fall asleep, but research in sleep medicine has consistently found that it disrupts the second half of the night. In the first few hours, it tends to suppress REM sleep, the stage linked to dreaming and memory. As your body clears the alcohol, there's a rebound: lighter, more broken sleep, more awakenings, and often a faster heart rate and more sweating. Alcohol also relaxes the throat muscles, which can make snoring and sleep apnea worse. Our [guide to alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) goes into the research in more detail.

### What diphenhydramine does to your sleep

Diphenhydramine makes you drowsy, but the evidence that it produces good-quality sleep is weak. A few things are worth knowing:

- **Tolerance builds quickly.** Studies of diphenhydramine for insomnia have found that its sedating effect fades after just a few nights of regular use. Major sleep medicine guidelines, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's guideline on chronic insomnia, do not recommend it as a long-term insomnia treatment because the evidence of benefit is small.
- **It lingers.** Diphenhydramine's half-life (the time it takes the body to clear half of a dose) is roughly 4 to 9 hours in healthy adults, and longer in older adults. That's why so many people feel hungover the morning after a sleep aid, even without drinking.
- **It doesn't restore normal sleep structure.** It sedates you. It doesn't undo alcohol's effects on REM sleep or the rebound waking.

Put together, ZzzQuil on top of alcohol gives you more sedation, more grogginess, and more risk, without fixing the underlying problem. You're likely to wake up feeling worse, not better.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take ZzzQuil?

There is no official waiting period printed on the label, and anyone who quotes you a precise number of hours that applies to everyone is guessing. What you can say with confidence:

- **Wait until the alcohol has fully cleared.** As a rough rule, the body processes about one standard drink per hour, but this varies a lot by body size, sex, food, genetics and how much you drank. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood the next morning.
- **If you're still feeling any effect of the alcohol, it's too soon.** Feeling tipsy, buzzed, or "a bit off" means alcohol is still in your system.
- **After a big night, the practical answer is "not tonight."** If you've had more than a couple of drinks, the safest choice is to skip the sleep aid altogether and use it, if you need it, on another night.
- **Using ZzzQuil on a later, alcohol-free night is generally fine** for healthy adults who follow the label. The concern is having both in your body at the same time.

The reverse question comes up too: **if you took ZzzQuil, how long should you wait before drinking?** Because diphenhydramine can stay active for many hours, it's sensible not to drink for at least the rest of that day. If you took a dose late at night and feel groggy the next afternoon, the drug is still having an effect, and alcohol will stack on top of it.

## Watch Out for Hidden Diphenhydramine and Doxylamine

Many people accidentally double up because sleep ingredients are hidden in products with very different names. If you're already sedated from drinking, this is easy to do. Before taking anything at night, check the Drug Facts box for these ingredients:

| Product type | Common examples | Sleep ingredient |
|---|---|---|
| Sleep aids | ZzzQuil Nighttime, Unisom SleepGels, store-brand "sleep aid" | Diphenhydramine |
| Sleep aids | Unisom SleepTabs, some store brands | Doxylamine |
| Nighttime cold and flu | NyQuil and many store-brand nighttime formulas | Doxylamine (plus acetaminophen in many) |
| "PM" painkillers | Tylenol PM, Advil PM, Aleve PM | Diphenhydramine |
| Allergy medicine | Benadryl | Diphenhydramine |
| Topical creams and sprays | Some anti-itch products | Diphenhydramine |

Doxylamine isn't the same drug as diphenhydramine, but it's from the same sedating antihistamine family and carries the same alcohol warning. Taking ZzzQuil on top of NyQuil, Tylenol PM or Benadryl means taking two sedating antihistamines at once.

There's another trap in the "PM" painkillers. Products like Tylenol PM add acetaminophen, which has its own serious interaction with alcohol in the liver. Our [guide to Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains that risk in detail. The short version is that a "PM" painkiller after drinking stacks a sedative problem on top of a liver problem.

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

The ZzzQuil and alcohol combination carries more risk if you:

- **Are over 65.** Older adults clear diphenhydramine more slowly and are more sensitive to its confusing and fall-causing effects.
- **Take other sedating medicines.** This includes benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, muscle relaxants, some antidepressants, some antipsychotics, gabapentin and pregabalin, other antihistamines, and prescription sleep medicines. Combining several sedatives with alcohol is where the risk of breathing problems becomes serious.
- **Have sleep apnea or breathing problems.** Both alcohol and sedatives can make breathing during sleep worse.
- **Have glaucoma or an enlarged prostate.** Diphenhydramine's anticholinergic effects can worsen both, and the label tells you to ask a doctor first.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** Ask your doctor before using any sleep aid, and avoid alcohol.
- **Will need to drive or work early the next day.** Next-day impairment from diphenhydramine is common, and alcohol adds to it.
- **Drink heavily on a regular basis.** If you find that you can't sleep without drinking, or can't sleep after drinking without a pill, that pattern deserves a doctor's input rather than a stronger sleep aid.

If any of these apply to you, a five-minute conversation with a pharmacist is worth it. They can look at your full medication list and tell you what's safe. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) also covers how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements.

## What About Melatonin-Based ZzzQuil Pure Zzzs?

ZzzQuil Pure Zzzs products are built around [melatonin](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol), a hormone your body makes to signal that it's time to sleep. Melatonin works differently from diphenhydramine. It mainly nudges the timing of sleep rather than heavily sedating you, and it doesn't have anticholinergic side effects.

That doesn't mean it pairs well with alcohol. Alcohol itself has been shown in research to lower the body's natural melatonin release, and adding a melatonin supplement doesn't undo alcohol's disruption of the second half of the night. Melatonin can also cause drowsiness, headaches and dizziness, and these can add to alcohol's effects. Many of the Pure Zzzs blends also include botanicals like valerian, which has mild sedating effects of its own.

A melatonin product is a gentler option than diphenhydramine, but the same basic advice applies: it's better not to combine any sleep product with alcohol, and to ask your doctor if you take other medicines. Supplements like melatonin also aren't regulated as tightly as drugs, so actual doses can differ from what's on the label.

## What to Do Instead When You Can't Sleep After Drinking

If you've had a few drinks and you're lying awake, the goal is to get through the night safely rather than to force sleep with medication. These steps are boring, but they help more than a pill would:

1. **Drink water before bed and keep some by the bed.** Alcohol makes you lose more fluid, and dehydration can add to night sweats, headaches and restless sleep.
2. **Stop drinking earlier in the evening.** The closer your last drink is to bedtime, the more alcohol will still be in your body during the night, and the worse the rebound waking tends to be. Giving yourself a few hours between your last drink and bed helps.
3. **Eat something.** Food slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed. Drinking on an empty stomach tends to cause a sharper peak and a rougher night.
4. **Keep the room cool and dark.** Alcohol can raise your heart rate and make you sweat. A cooler room helps.
5. **Skip the late-night screen scroll.** Bright light late at night pushes back your body clock.
6. **If you wake at 3 a.m., don't fight it.** Get up briefly, keep lights low, have some water, and go back to bed when you feel sleepy. Lying there frustrated rarely helps.
7. **Sleep on your side if you've had a lot to drink.** If you feel at all nauseous, this lowers the risk of choking if you vomit. If someone else has had a lot to drink, help them onto their side and don't leave them alone.
8. **Accept a shorter night.** One poor night of sleep is unpleasant but not dangerous. Mixing sedatives with alcohol can be.

For the bigger picture of how drinking interacts with your body clock, see our guide on [sleep optimization for social drinkers](/never-hungover/sleep-optimization-social-drinkers-circadian-rhythm). And if poor sleep is a regular part of the morning after, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the drinking habits with the best evidence behind them.

## Where DHM Fits In (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people look at supplements to make drinking nights a bit easier on the body. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*) that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. A widely cited 2012 study in rats, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, found that DHM counteracted some of alcohol's effects on GABA receptors in the brain. Most of the research so far comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not settled.

Here's what DHM is not:

- **It is not a sleep aid**, and it should not be treated as a substitute for one.
- **It does not make it safe to combine ZzzQuil or any sedative with alcohol.** There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the combined sedating effect of diphenhydramine and alcohol.
- **It does not lower your blood alcohol level enough to make driving safe** or to change anything in this article's safety advice.

Because DHM acts on GABA receptors, the same system that alcohol and many sedatives affect, it's sensible to ask a doctor or pharmacist before using it if you take sedatives, sleep medicines, or anti-anxiety medicines.

If you're a healthy adult who wants to try DHM on nights you drink, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Treat it as one small part of a sensible drinking night, alongside water, food, and pacing, and never as a reason to mix alcohol with sleep medicine.

## The Bottom Line

- ZzzQuil Nighttime Sleep-Aid contains diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine. Its label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks while using it.
- The standard ZzzQuil liquid is made without alcohol, unlike original NyQuil. But that doesn't make it safe to take after drinking, because the problem is the diphenhydramine plus the alcohol already in your body.
- Together, they cause additive sedation, poorer coordination, more confusion, and a groggier morning. At high doses or after heavy drinking, the risks include choking on vomit and slowed breathing.
- ZzzQuil doesn't fix alcohol's damage to sleep. It adds sedation without restoring normal sleep, and tolerance to it builds within days.
- If you've been drinking tonight, skip the sleep aid. Wait until the alcohol has fully cleared, and check every product for hidden diphenhydramine or doxylamine.
- If someone who mixed alcohol and a sleep aid is hard to wake, breathing slowly, vomiting while drowsy, or confused, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take ZzzQuil after drinking alcohol?**

It's best not to. ZzzQuil Nighttime Sleep-Aid contains diphenhydramine, and its label says to avoid alcoholic drinks while using it. Both diphenhydramine and alcohol slow down your brain, so together they cause stronger sedation, poorer coordination, more confusion and a groggier morning than either alone. After heavy drinking, the combination can be dangerous. Wait until the alcohol has fully cleared, and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Does ZzzQuil have alcohol in it?**

The standard ZzzQuil Nighttime Sleep-Aid liquid is made without alcohol, and the LiquiCaps don't contain drinking alcohol either. That's different from the original NyQuil liquid, which lists alcohol as an inactive ingredient. Formulas can change, so check the inactive ingredients on your own package. Either way, being alcohol-free doesn't make ZzzQuil safe to take after drinking, because the diphenhydramine is what interacts with alcohol.

**How long after drinking can I take ZzzQuil?**

There's no official waiting period. A sensible approach is to wait until the alcohol is completely out of your system. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot. If you still feel any effect of alcohol, it's too soon. After a heavy night, the safest choice is to skip ZzzQuil that night entirely.

**What happens if you mix ZzzQuil and alcohol?**

Most commonly, you'll feel much more sedated and uncoordinated than expected and wake up groggy, with poor concentration. Memory can be affected, so you might forget you took a dose. With larger amounts, the risks include falls, vomiting while too sedated to wake properly (which can cause choking), and slowed breathing. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or is very confused, call 911.

**Is one drink and ZzzQuil dangerous?**

For a healthy adult, one drink and a normal dose of ZzzQuil is unlikely to be life-threatening, but it will usually cause more drowsiness and next-day grogginess than you'd expect, and the label still advises avoiding alcohol. The risk is higher if you're older, take other sedating medicines, have sleep apnea or breathing problems, or need to drive the next morning. When in doubt, skip the sleep aid that night.

**Can I take ZzzQuil the night after drinking to fix my sleep?**

Once the alcohol has fully cleared, a healthy adult can generally use ZzzQuil as directed on a later night. But it won't repair the sleep alcohol disrupted, and tolerance to diphenhydramine builds within a few nights of regular use. If you find you need a sleep aid after most nights you drink, talk to your doctor, since frequent use isn't recommended and the pattern is worth looking at.

**Is ZzzQuil Pure Zzzs melatonin safe with alcohol?**

Melatonin is gentler than diphenhydramine and doesn't have the same anticholinergic side effects, but combining it with alcohol still isn't a good idea. Alcohol lowers your body's natural melatonin and disrupts the second half of the night, and a melatonin supplement doesn't undo that. Melatonin can also cause drowsiness and dizziness that add to alcohol's effects. Ask a doctor if you take other medicines.

**Is ZzzQuil the same as Benadryl or NyQuil?**

ZzzQuil Nighttime Sleep-Aid and Benadryl both contain diphenhydramine, so taking them together means doubling up on the same drug. NyQuil is a cold and flu medicine that contains a different sedating antihistamine, doxylamine, and usually acetaminophen as well. All three carry alcohol warnings, and none should be combined with each other or taken after drinking.

**Does DHM make it safe to take ZzzQuil with alcohol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the combined sedating effect of diphenhydramine and alcohol, and it doesn't change any of the safety advice here. DHM is not a sleep aid. Because it acts on GABA receptors, ask a doctor before using it if you take sedatives or sleep medicines.
